power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P=.78", Sentence = "No difference in discrimination between Black and White patients was detected (Table 4; AUROC 0.6948 vs 0.6976; difference 0.0029, 95% CI -0.0184 to 0.0237; P=.78), but the interval does not exclude differences of up to about 0.02, so this is not evidence of equivalence."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 144 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 1088 files: 375 data, 465 code, 26 documentation, 213 materials, 2 output, 7 unknown.
-  We found 12 tabular data files and extracted 492 columns from 10 of them.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 492 columns across 70 data files.
#### Issues Identified

6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Audit_207]", "supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Model_Comparison_OOF]", "supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Timestamp_Audit]", "thiagobandeira1/Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-v16.1-jamia.zip/thiagobandeira1-Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-f1f90fa/supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Audit_207]", "thiagobandeira1/Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-v16.1-jamia.zip/thiagobandeira1-Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-f1f90fa/supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Model_Comparison_OOF]", "thiagobandeira1/Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-v16.1-jamia.zip/thiagobandeira1-Medicare-30day-Readmission-MIMIC-IV-f1f90fa/supplementary/Supplementary Appendix 1 Predictor Audit and Selection.xlsx [Timestamp_Audit]" ), Column = c("verified_definition_v8", "n_features", "verified_definition", "verified_definition_v8", "n_features", "verified_definition" ), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 89 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 80% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"per-fold [38, ...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 88 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 89 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 80% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"per-fold [38, ...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 88 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ..." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 70 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.
